title: Candle Inclusion
summary: Merging candles that contain one another — the first step behind every Chan structure
body:
Raw candles often have one bar fully engulfing the previous one, or the reverse. This is called an **inclusion relationship**, and it blurs fractal detection, so Chan merges these bars away first.

The test is simple: for two adjacent candles, if A's high is not below B's high and A's low is not above B's low, they are in an inclusion relationship.

The merge direction depends on the **prevailing trend**:

• Processing upward, take the higher of the two highs and the higher of the two lows
• Processing downward, take the lower of the two lows and the lower of the two highs

The direction is decided by the bar *before* the two being merged — this trips people up. It's not where price goes after the merge; it's the trend heading into this stretch.

The resulting sequence is called **merged candles**, and everything later — fractals, strokes, segments — is built on top of it. The candles you see on the chart are still the raw ones, but the structure lines are drawn on the merged result, so an endpoint may occasionally look like it doesn't line up with a wick. That's normal.

**How this app does it**

Inclusion is handled by the rule above. The direction comes from the move before the two bars being merged: if, of the two preceding merged candles, the later one has the higher high, merge upward; if lower, merge downward.

All prices are **split- and dividend-adjusted**, so gaps created by corporate actions aren't mistaken for structure.

The chart still shows the original candles; structure lines are drawn on the merged result. Candles before the first stroke forms don't take part in any structure.

title: Fractal
summary: A local high or low made of three merged candles — the endpoint of a stroke
body:
A fractal is the smallest structural unit in Chan, formed by **three consecutive merged candles**.

**Top fractal**: the middle bar's high is the highest of the three, and its low is also the highest of the three.

**Bottom fractal**: the middle bar's low is the lowest of the three, and its high is also the lowest of the three.

Both conditions must hold. A bar with the highest high but not the highest low is not a top fractal — this detail is what makes fractals reliable.

A fractal on its own is **not a trading signal**. It's only a candidate turning point; whether it holds depends on whether a stroke follows. On the chart, top fractals are red and bottom fractals green, there to locate structure endpoints — not to signal.

In practice fractals often get "broken": a bottom fractal forms, the next bar makes a new low, and the fractal is voided. That's why unconfirmed structure is drawn with dashed lines.

**How this app does it**

A top fractal requires the middle candle's high and low to both be strictly above its neighbors'; a bottom fractal is the mirror image — exactly the definition above.

The chart **only marks fractals that became stroke endpoints**. Candidate fractals that haven't produced a stroke can be invalidated at any time, and showing them would just add noise. Structure at the right edge that later candles haven't confirmed yet is marked as pending.

title: Stroke
summary: The move between a top fractal and a bottom fractal, with at least one candle in between
body:
A stroke connects adjacent top and bottom fractals — the first structure in Chan with a direction.

Two conditions:

• The endpoints must be one top and one bottom, in opposite directions
• The two fractals must have **at least one independent merged candle between them** (versions differ on the count; a common rule is "fractals share no candle and there is at least one in between")

The second condition is key. It filters out the noise of price flicking back and forth over one or two bars. Without it, the slightest chop would draw a mess of strokes.

Strokes are up or down: bottom fractal → top fractal is an up-stroke, and the reverse a down-stroke. They're drawn in blue.

**Strokes can disappear.** If later price makes a new high or low, the original fractal breaks and its stroke ceases to exist. So the rightmost stroke is usually dashed — it hasn't been confirmed by later price yet.

**How this app does it**

A stroke is valid only when all of these hold:

• Its ends are one top and one bottom, in opposite directions
• The two fractals share no candles: counting from the left candle of the starting fractal to the right candle of the ending fractal gives at least **6** merged candles
• The price ranges of the two fractals don't contain one another

The endpoint is the **most extreme** fractal after the start: the highest top for an up-stroke, the lowest bottom for a down-stroke. When price keeps making new highs or lows, the last stroke **extends** to the new extreme — which is why the last stroke is always treated as pending.

title: Segment
summary: A higher-degree structure of at least three strokes that share an overlapping range
body:
The stroke is the smallest directional unit; the segment is the next level up that organizes strokes.

The basic requirement: **a segment is made of at least three strokes**, and those strokes must share an overlapping price range. Three strokes with no overlap are just a one-way move, not a segment.

Deciding when a segment ends is one of the trickiest parts of Chan; the common approach checks whether the "characteristic sequence" forms a fractal. Simply put: an up-segment's characteristic sequence is built from the highs and lows of its down-strokes, and when that sequence forms a top fractal, the segment may be ending.

In practice, just remember what a segment does: **it filters out noise at the stroke level**. Strokes can change several times a day; segments are far steadier, and pivots are defined at the segment level.

Segments are drawn in orange, a bit thicker than the blue strokes. Read the segment direction first, then the stroke detail — reverse the order and short-term swings will mislead you.

**How this app does it**

A segment consists of at least **3 strokes**, takes its direction from the first stroke, and ends according to the feature sequence: for an up-segment, its down-strokes form the feature sequence; once inclusion is handled and a top fractal appears there, the segment is considered finished (mirror for down-segments).

When the feature sequence has a gap, the app doesn't conclude immediately — it looks at the next few strokes for confirmation, so segments aren't cut short. A segment never swallows its own starting point. The last segment is marked pending until later moves confirm it.

title: Pivot (Hub)
summary: The overlap of three consecutive moves — the core of how Chan tells trend from range
body:
The pivot is the core concept of Chan. Definition: **the overlapping price range of three consecutive sub-degree moves**.

At the stroke level, it's the overlap of three consecutive strokes; at the segment level, the overlap of three consecutive segments. Take each move's high and low: the pivot's upper bound (ZG) is the highest of the three lows, and its lower bound (ZD) is the lowest of the three highs. If the upper bound is below the lower bound, there is no pivot.

The pivot matters because it **defines the balance zone between buyers and sellers**. Price oscillating inside means little disagreement; price leaving and not returning means one side has gained the upper hand.

From this come two basic move types:

• **Range**: a single pivot, with price moving in and out of it repeatedly
• **Trend**: two or more pivots in the same direction, each fully clearing the previous one

Pivots are drawn as purple rectangles. **Whether a pivot is broken, and whether a pullback confirms the break, matters more than any single buy/sell point.**

**How this app does it**

**Stroke-level pivot**: starting from a stroke, consecutive strokes whose prices overlap are grouped together; a group needs **at least 3 strokes** to count as a pivot. The upper bound ZG is the lowest of the first three strokes' highs and the lower bound ZD is the highest of their lows — and they **stay fixed** afterwards; only the extremes GG and DD update as the pivot extends. After price leaves the pivot, if the stroke back can't reach the pivot range (a rebound peaking below ZD, or a pullback bottoming above ZG), a new group begins.

**Segment-level pivot**: the overlap of three consecutive segments; later segments that still overlap that range extend it.

**Trend type**: two or more pivots stepping higher (each one's ZD above the previous one's ZG) is an uptrend, stepping lower is a downtrend, anything else is a consolidation. Segment-level pivots take priority when present.

title: Divergence
summary: Price makes a new high or low but with less force than the prior leg — a key turning-point hint
body:
Divergence means a move makes a **new high or low** while the **force driving it actually shrinks**.

Two common ways to gauge force:

• **Area ratio**: compare the MACD histogram area of two same-direction legs; the later leg's area is clearly smaller than the earlier one's
• **Slope**: the later leg's price changes more slowly than the earlier one's

The "area ratio" shown on the app's signal cards is the first method. A value below 1 means the later leg is weaker — the smaller it is, the clearer the divergence.

Divergence must be compared between two legs of the **same degree, same direction, with a pivot in between**. Comparing arbitrary legs is meaningless.

**Divergence is not a reversal.** It only says the current direction is running out of force; what follows may reverse, or may just consolidate sideways and continue. Its value is telling you "don't chase here," not "flip your position here."

Force fading inside a range is usually called "consolidation divergence," less reliable than trend divergence.

**How this app does it**

Divergence is used in two places:

• **Whether a type-1 buy/sell exists**: look at the last 5 to 21 strokes — the first stroke holds the high of the stretch, the last one makes a new low (mirror for sells), and the last stroke's **price range** is weaker than the earlier declines, with **volume** or **duration** also weaker. Only then has the move run out of force.
• **How strong the divergence is**: measured with MACD (see the next lesson). The area must shrink **and** the DIF line must fail to make a new extreme — both conditions together confirm a divergence.

The app compares **adjacent same-direction strokes** and doesn't strictly require a pivot in between — a practical simplification. If two or more pivots have formed before the current stroke it counts as a trend divergence; otherwise, a consolidation divergence.

title: MACD & Area Ratio
summary: What the sub-chart at the bottom of the analysis page is, and how the signal card's "area ratio" is computed
body:
The panel below the chart on the analysis page is **MACD**. It isn't native to Chan, but this app uses it to **quantify the force of a divergence** — the "area ratio" on the signal cards comes from here.

It has three parts:

• **DIF** (blue line): the difference between a fast and a slow moving average, showing short- vs. medium-term deviation
• **DEA** (orange line): a moving average of DIF, smoother and slower to react
• **Histogram**: DIF minus DEA; positive bars in green, negative in red

The bars are the most intuitive part. **Longer bars mean the current direction is accelerating; shorter bars mean it's decelerating**, and bars crossing the zero line mean short-term momentum has changed direction.

Note that shrinking bars do **not** mean price is falling — only that the rise is slowing. Price still making new highs while the bars already shrink is the classic shape of a divergence.

**How the area ratio is derived**

Sum each same-direction leg's MACD histogram area and divide the later by the earlier — that's the **area ratio** on the signal card.

• Below 1: the later leg is weaker; the smaller it is, the clearer the divergence
• Near or above 1: force hasn't faded, so it isn't a divergence

The comparison must be between two legs of the **same degree, same direction, with a pivot in between**; a number from two arbitrary legs is meaningless.

**MACD is only a measuring tool, not a trading signal.** Shrinking bars only say the current direction is fading; whether it reverses or continues after a pause, they can't tell you.

**How this app does it**

Parameters are the common **12 / 26 / 9**.

A stroke's area is the sum of the absolute MACD bar lengths between its start and end; the area ratio is the current stroke's area divided by the previous same-direction stroke's. It's only computed when price makes a new high or low.

Divergence strength has three bands: **below 0.4 is strong, 0.4–0.7 medium, 0.7–1 weak**. If the area shrinks but DIF still makes a new extreme, momentum is actually stronger, so it doesn't count as divergence.

title: The Three Buy/Sell Points
summary: Chan groups timing into three types, each tied to a different stage of the trend
body:
Chan groups buy points into three types, with sell points mirrored.

**1st buy**: the low where the move diverges after the last pivot of a downtrend. It's the theoretical bottom, but also the hardest to judge — divergence can be voided by later price at any time, and 1st-buy failures are common.

**2nd buy**: after the 1st buy bounces, price pulls back again but **doesn't make a new low**. One more confirmation than the 1st buy, so lower risk, at the cost of a higher entry.

**3rd buy**: after price breaks above the pivot's upper bound, the point where the pullback **no longer falls back into the pivot**. This is the signal that a trend is established — the highest certainty, but already far from the bottom.

The three buy points are a **trade-off between certainty and price**: the 1st buy is cheap but uncertain, the 3rd buy expensive but solid.

The app's "Signals" tab lists detected buy/sell points, their level and strength. **These are structure-detection results, not investment advice** — the same spot can be an opposite signal at a different degree, and which degree to use depends on your holding horizon.

**How this app does it**

• **Type-1 buy/sell**: identified with the force rule from the Divergence lesson. Strength comes from that stroke's MACD divergence; if MACD doesn't confirm a divergence, it's marked weak.
• **Type-2 buy/sell**: the end of a pullback stroke (at least 7 merged candles) overlaps in price with the endpoints of at least 2 similarly long strokes among the previous 8 — the pullback landed on a support (or resistance) zone built by earlier turning points, without a new low (high).
• **Type-3 buy/sell**: take the last 5 strokes and treat the overlap of strokes 1 and 3 (same direction as stroke 5) as a pivot. If stroke 5's pullback low stays above that pivot's top, and the 34-period moving average at the ends of strokes 1, 3 and 5 is stepping higher, it's a type-3 buy (mirror for sells).

Every signal is **evaluated candle by candle using only the data available at that time**, and placed at the end of its stroke. If that stroke later extends because price kept making new lows or highs, the signal is treated as failed and no longer shown.

Type-2 and type-3 strength reflects the degree of the most recent completed pivot before the signal (segment level outranks stroke level) and how far the retracement stayed from the pivot boundary.

title: Trend Levels
summary: Level is set by pivots, not by candle timeframe — the most common misconception
body:
Level is the most misunderstood concept in Chan.

**Level is not the candle timeframe.** A small-degree move can appear on a daily chart, and a large-degree structure can form on a 5-minute chart. Level is set by the **hierarchy of pivots**: a pivot made of strokes is one level, a pivot made of segments is the next level up, and so on recursively.

In practice people approximate level with timeframe, for convenience:

• 5-min / 30-min — intraday
• Daily — swing
• Weekly — medium-to-long term

This approximation is good enough most of the time, but know it's only an approximation.

The real point of level is to **decide which layer's signals to watch**. A daily-level 1st buy may show up as a whole down-leg on the 30-minute; a 30-minute 3rd buy may be nothing on the daily.

**A signal must match your holding horizon.** Using a 5-minute buy point for a long-term hold, or a weekly buy point for intraday, is using the tool in the wrong place. The app's daily/weekly switch is switching exactly this layer.

**How this app does it**

The analysis page switches between **daily and weekly**; weekly candles are built from daily ones. Within one timeframe there are two layers: stroke-level pivots capture the smaller swings, segment-level pivots the larger structure. In the pattern read-out, the last stroke's direction stands for the short-term rhythm and the segment direction for the larger trend, which carries more weight.

So the structure doesn't drift with the start date you pick, the app pulls extra history before the visible range (about 180 days for daily, 540 for weekly), computes on the whole series, then shows only the visible part.
